clues.title: Google car: low camera, big blur, black-white car
text: The appearance of the standard Japanese Google car is often **black and white**. You may find it in [black](https://www.google.com/maps/@39.545526,140.3963943,3a,75y,199.92h,63.31t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1sULSsNXwYSpwiLMrI-UT9Sg!2e0!5s20120901T000000!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu) or rarely with an [antenna](https://goo.gl/maps/4eZr42n9iQuCjk9f9).
In addition, due to privacy reasons, the camera is intentionally set lower to the ground. This is known as **low-cam**. You can identify it by:
- Looking downwards. The blur will be noticeably larger.
- The road will look wider, and objects will be viewed from a lower perspective.

NOTE: The only other country that always has low-cam is [Switzerland](https://goo.gl/maps/NgSfAc8sDEh4reQy7). It can also be seen in Generation 4 coverage in [Sri Lanka](https://goo.gl/maps/DisPbnfvKkJdXc3TA). Also, the car will be blurred in Switzerland.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The car is often black and white, rarely with an antenna. The camera sits low, so the car blur is big and the road looks wide from a low angle. Switzerland is always low-cam too, but its car is blurred out.

differs.how: Swiss car is blurred out; Japan's is visible

clues.title: Driving side: left
text: Japan drives on the **left** **hand **side of the road.
NOTE: Hong Kong drives on the left hand side of the road, same as Japan. South Korea and Taiwan drive on the right hand side instead.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Traffic drives on the left. Hong Kong does too; South Korea and Taiwan drive on the right.

differs.how: South Korea drives on the right

clues.title: Language: kanji plus looped hiragana
text: Japanese is written with a mixture of **three main systems**: kanji and two syllabic scripts: hiragana and katakana. Formal signs and texts will mostly use kanji and hiragana. The kanji system is directly borrowed from Chinese and thus looks very similar, while the syllabic scripts are more loosely inspired by Chinese. Hiragana generally looks simpler than Chinese characters, many of the symbols have loops, which are not present in Chinese. The shapes are also typically slightly softer than the shapes present in most kanji.
_You can learn more about hiragana, katakana and kanji in the region guessing section, learning frequent terms and names._

images.caption: Japanese text with kanji and hiragana

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Japanese mixes kanji (like Chinese characters), hiragana (simpler, soft and looped) and katakana. Signs mostly use kanji and hiragana.

clues.title: Language: katakana, simple angular shapes
text: Katakana is mainly used for loan words, and are thus common to find in commercials. They are generally quite simple, with a lot of geometrical shapes rather than the more artistic shapes present in hiragana and kanji.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Katakana is used mainly for foreign words and is common in adverts. It uses simple, geometric shapes, less artistic than hiragana and kanji.

clues.title: Pole: round concrete with screw-like steps
text: Japan mostly uses these **round concrete** poles, which have these screw-like extensions. Other information can often be found on or attached to the pole including:
- Electrical plates.
- Guy-wires.
- Pole reflectors.
Therefore, they are a key asset in region guessing Japan.
_You can learn more about plates, reflectors, and guy-wires in the region guessing section._

images.caption: Red circles zoom in on the screw-like steps and the yellow-black band on the round concrete pole

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Round concrete poles with screw-like extensions, usually with electrical plates, guy wires or reflectors attached. Key objects for finding the region.

clues.title: Pole: short reflector, yellow or white stripes
text: You can find a variety of pole reflectors in Japan. They are typically short and **do not **touch the ground. Common patterns found all across Japan include:
- Yellow [vertical stripes](https://goo.gl/maps/7BqmnkTQC1MVKsfy7).
- Yellow [diagonal stripes](https://goo.gl/maps/y7e5UtxMuFbPtM2LA).
- Vertical or diagonal [white stripes](https://maps.app.goo.gl/9oGeT8mpLgDfZjYK7).

NOTE: The [Taiwanese variant](https://goo.gl/maps/t6yb5Q4LZtRinPRQ7) has diagonal stripes that reach the ground. The [South Korean ones](https://goo.gl/maps/pcSbJznpLXenKtWX9) have diagonal, thicker stripes.
_You can learn more about the different regional reflectors in the region guessing section._

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Reflectors on poles are short and don't touch the ground, with yellow vertical or diagonal stripes, or white stripes. Taiwan's diagonal stripes reach the ground; South Korea's are thicker.

differs.how: South Korea's diagonal stripes are thicker

clues.title: Plate: short white with green text
text: Japan uses a standard **short white** licence plate with green text. You will often see a different short yellow version with black text issued to “light automobiles”, otherwise known as Kei Cars.

images.caption: Japanese plates: standard white (top) and yellow kei car (bottom)

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Short white plates with green text. Light cars (Kei cars) have short yellow plates with black text.

clues.title: Road lines: white edges, never yellow edges
text: Japan has three common variations of road lines. They are as follows:
- The most common being white, solid outer lines with a [dashed white](https://goo.gl/maps/ydLiQ19hdgbTekD86) middle line.
- White solid sidelines with a [yellow solid](https://goo.gl/maps/mPCxbst43hVaZXcP6) middle line.
- White solid sidelines with [yellow and white](https://goo.gl/maps/Vcdsq6sH8EQkhnUp6) middle lines.
While you may find other, more rare combinations, Japan will never have yellow outside road lines.

images.caption: Red circles mark the line colours in three shots: dashed white, solid yellow, and white with yellow

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Three common styles: white edges with a dashed white middle (most common), white edges with solid yellow middle, or white edges with yellow and white middle lines. Edge lines are never yellow.

clues.title: Bollard: white with round reflectors
text: Japan usually uses simple white bollards with **circular reflector(s)** on the top. However, sometimes these bollards are [black](https://goo.gl/maps/cejvLnBS8MeHHbuU8), or have [other extensions](https://goo.gl/maps/DaSsHqZhpkmU3Duq8). They can also have the city or prefecture written on it in kanji.
_You can learn more about the bollards and kanji in the region guessing section._

images.caption: White poles topped by an orange or grey ball, with the circle zooming in on the prefecture name written on the post

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Usually simple white bollards with round reflectors on top. Sometimes black or with extras, and some have the city or prefecture written in kanji.

clues.title: Guardrail: simple white
text: Japan generally uses these simple, **white** guardrails.
_You can learn more about the exceptions in the region guessing section._

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Guardrails are generally simple and white.

clues.title: Route marker: hexagonal prefecture shield
text: Prefecture roads are identified by their **hexagonal-shaped** shields. The prefecture is often written under the road number in kanji. While the shield design remains, other variations can be found:
- On [prefectural highway shields](https://goo.gl/maps/6PsFbdz9gtDyGWbs9) (with kanji).
- On directional [intersection](https://goo.gl/maps/jsWfsJUW3r7JjE8v5) signs.
- Or on small, directional [arrow](https://goo.gl/maps/WrtbZh2DYQ6B4YYh7) signs.
As multiple prefectures can have the same road number, it is recommended to first find the prefecture you are in.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Prefecture roads use hexagonal shields, often with the prefecture in kanji under the number. Different prefectures reuse the same road numbers.

clues.title: Sign: unique stop sign, mirrors, school crossing
text: Some frequently seen infrastructure in Japan consists of:
- This unique [stop sign](https://goo.gl/maps/RYbbcM52HxH5rjvB6).
- A school [pedestrian crossing](https://maps.app.goo.gl/kp1Biy8pumCZtfsu5).
- And these traffic [mirrors](https://goo.gl/maps/RvMvRRrnmGWL4Z9CA).
While many infrastructural clues exist, these three are very common, and may very well help you identify Japan on a difficult round.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Three common sights: a unique stop sign, a school pedestrian crossing, and traffic mirrors at junctions.

clues.title: Wall: retaining walls in rural areas
text: **Retaining walls** can be an excellent clue for Japan in rural areas with little to no information.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Retaining walls are a good clue in rural areas with little else to go on.

clues.title: Phone numbers: area codes rise going south
text: **Area codes** are commonly found throughout the country and increase to the south.
NOTE: Area codes ending with a 0 are often not regional, most notably 0120.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Area codes get larger further south. Codes ending in 0, such as 0120, are usually not regional.

clues.title: Pole: orange arrow above the top plate
text: You may sometimes find an **orange arrow** located above the top most pole plate in Chugoku.

images.caption: The inset circle zooms in on the orange arrow above the top plate

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In the Chugoku region, you may see an orange arrow above the top pole plate.

clues.title: Pole: orange and black bands around the pole
text: These **orange and black bands **wrapped around poles can often be found in Shikoku.

images.caption: The inset circle zooms in on the orange and black bands around the pole

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Orange-and-black bands wrapped around poles are often found in Shikoku.

clues.title: Pole: 120-degree angled arm
text: These attachments with an approximately **120-degree angle **can commonly be found on poles in Kansai.
NOTE: Sometimes there is no angle, and instead just an [angled downward attachment](https://maps.app.goo.gl/LM3HD3nFCYj27xMUA).

images.caption: The inset circle zooms in on the arm angled at 120 degrees

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Attachments with an angle of about 120 degrees are common on poles in Kansai. Sometimes just an arm angled downward.

clues.title: Pole: small 90-degree angled arm
text: These smaller attachments with a **90-degree angle **can commonly be found on poles in Shikoku.

images.caption: The inset circle zooms in on the small arm angled at 90 degrees

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Smaller attachments with a 90-degree angle are common on poles in Shikoku.

clues.title: Pole: transformer on plus-shaped bar or two bars
text: The electrical poles in Hokkaido either have this [**plus-shaped bar**](https://maps.app.goo.gl/vxrc8aYqGXDnmM5HA) attached to the **side** of the pole, or one transformer mounted on [**two bars**](https://maps.app.goo.gl/ySYEqmRFjMEMEwhc7).
However, if there is more than one transformer, they will often be mounted on the sides of a **square**.
NOTE: While the Kanto transformer may also be mounted on two bars, Hokkaido will never have a wooden plate.

images.caption: Pole transformers mounted on a plus-shaped bar or two bars

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Hokkaido, poles have a plus-shaped bar on the side, or a transformer on two bars. Several transformers are usually on the sides of a square. The Kanto one may also use two bars, but Hokkaido never has a wooden plate.

clues.title: Pole: transformer on round plate with zigzag bar
text: The transformers in Tohoku, which often have additional square holding brackets and the logo of the Tohoku Electrical Company, are sometimes mounted on a **round plate** with a **zigzag bar**.
Furthermore, you may also find transformers mounted on the **side** **of a** **square**, with a straight bar mounted on the top of the square. Rarely, you may find a square without a bar.
NOTE: While Kansai may have a square attachment as well, the bar will be mounted on the bottom rather than the top.

images.caption: Pole transformers mounted on a round plate with a zigzag bar

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Tohoku, transformers often have square holding brackets and the Tohoku Electric logo, sometimes on a round plate with a zigzag bar, or on a square with a straight bar on top. Kansai's square has the bar at the bottom.

clues.title: Pole: transformer on wooden plate and two bars
text: The transformers in Kanto, which can have [three](https://maps.app.goo.gl/UyMb991t8fkqFCwZ7) or [two insulators](https://maps.app.goo.gl/cKBTRWDiWHRFbbPw6), are often mounted on a [**wooden plate**](https://maps.app.goo.gl/yF8PkEfCbKfek7FTA) and two bars, or a [round plate](https://maps.app.goo.gl/7jHgmppBUEg2Po5w6) and a T-shaped bar.
NOTE: While the Hokkaido transformer may also be mounted on two bars, it will never have a wooden plate. Kanto ones can also be mounted without a wooden plate.

images.caption: Pole transformers on a wooden plate with two bars; the circle zooms in on one

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Kanto, transformers with two or three insulators are often on a wooden plate with two bars, or a round plate with a T-shaped bar. Hokkaido's can use two bars but never a wooden plate.

clues.title: Pole: transformer, lamp-shaped insulators
text: The transformers in Hokuriku, which are attached with thin metal bars, often have these [**small “lamp” shaped insulators**](https://maps.app.goo.gl/52GKXLANS9PNefQv9). There will **never** be a bar present except for the attachment mentioned above.
NOTE: The prefecture of Niigata will have the Tohoku transformer design, as opposed to Hokuriku one.

images.caption: Pole transformers with lamp-shaped insulators; the circle zooms in on one

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Hokuriku, transformers attach with thin metal bars and often have small lamp-shaped insulators; no other bar. Niigata uses the Tohoku design instead.

clues.title: Pole: transformer with yellow numbers, black taps
text: The transformers in Chubu, which often have painted **yellow numbers** and **black “tap” connectors**, are either attached with [**large** **triangle and horizontal bars**](https://maps.app.goo.gl/HGLz9BBt5ixtvtPCA), or these [**thin metal brackets**](https://maps.app.goo.gl/8kXAdcaVBaDhy2v56).

images.caption: Pole with transformers; a red circle zooms in on a transformer top with black taps

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Chubu, transformers often have painted yellow numbers and black tap connectors, attached with a big triangle and horizontal bars or thin metal brackets.

clues.title: Pole: transformer on square with bottom bar
text: The transformers in Kansai have either a **straight **or **zigzag bar** mounted on the **bottom** of a **square**. The transformer(s) will be mounted on the sides of that same square.
While this is uncommon, the bar and transformer(s) may be mounted on a [**vertical bar**](https://maps.app.goo.gl/kHToBhThugutvWjY9), rather than a square.
NOTE: While Tohoku may have a square attachment as well, the bar will be mounted on the **top** rather than the bottom.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Kansai, a straight or zigzag bar sits at the bottom of a square with the transformers on its sides, occasionally on a vertical bar. Tohoku's bar is on top.

clues.title: Pole: cross bar with full triangle, red numbers
text: The transformers in Chugoku, which have a **cross-shaped bar** attached in the **middle** of the pole, mounted by a **full triangle**, will have a **long horizontal **or [**short vertical**](https://maps.app.goo.gl/C47yQpCXaFeQ5sARA)** insulator(s)** at the end.
A white sticker will often be stuck to the bottom of the transformer with **red numbers**. They may also be painted on the **side**.

images.caption: Pole cross bars with insulators; red circles zoom in on the insulator clusters

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Chugoku, a cross-shaped bar in the middle of the pole on a full triangle, with long horizontal or short vertical insulators. A white sticker with red numbers is often under the transformer.

clues.title: Pole: cross bar, half triangle, hat insulators
text: The transformers in Shikoku, which also have a **cross-shaped bar **attached in the **middle** of the pole, mounted by a **half triangle**, will have [**“hat shaped”** **short horizontal insulators**](https://maps.app.goo.gl/kFzbZ6yh1rfAGQV88) at the end.
A white sticker will often be stuck to the bottom of the transformer with **black numbers**.

images.caption: Pole with cross bar and transformer; the red circle zooms in on hat-shaped insulators, top left

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Shikoku, a cross-shaped bar in the middle on a half triangle, with hat-shaped short horizontal insulators. A white sticker with black numbers is often under the transformer.

clues.title: Pole: transformers opposite sides, 3 insulators
text: The transformers in Kyushu, which have a **straight bar** attached on the **side** of the pole with **three insulators** at the end, will have transformers mounted **180-degrees** from one another.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Kyushu, a straight bar on the side of the pole with three insulators at the end, with transformers 180 degrees apart.

clues.title: Pole: T-bar, transformers on opposite sides
text: Transformers in Okinawa, which have a **T-shaped bar** attached on the **side** of the pole, will have transformers mounted on **opposite sides** of the pole.

images.caption: T-bar pole with transformers on opposite sides; the red circle highlights them, left

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Okinawa, a T-shaped bar on the side of the pole with transformers on opposite sides.

clues.title: Pole: grey insulator-like blocks
text: These **grey “insulator-esque” blocks**, which wires are fed through, can be found in the regions of Chubu, Kansai, Chugoku, Shikoku, and very rarely in Hokkaido.

images.caption: Transformer pole; red circles zoom in on grey insulator-like blocks

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Grey blocks like insulators, with wires fed through, appear in Chubu, Kansai, Chugoku and Shikoku, and very rarely Hokkaido.

clues.title: Pole: top with four thick bars and a circle
text: This pole top, with **four thicker bars** and a **circle** **piece** at the top, is common in the Chubu region.

images.caption: Pole in the distance; the red circle zooms in on a top with four thick bars and a circle

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A pole top with four thicker bars and a circle at the top is common in Chubu.

clues.title: Pole: tent-shaped top, sides filled in
text: This pole top, with **two sides filled in** and shaped like a **tent**, is common in the Hokuriku region.

images.caption: Pole in the distance; the red circle zooms in on a tent-shaped top with filled-in sides

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A pole top with two filled-in sides shaped like a tent is common in Hokuriku.

clues.title: Pole: top with four thin skinny bars
text: This pole top, with **four thin, skinny bars**, is common in the Chugoku region.

images.caption: Street with poles; the red circle zooms in on a pole top with four thin skinny bars
Two pole tops: a thin-topped pole on the left and a thicker one on the right

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A pole top with four thin, skinny bars is common in Chugoku.

clues.title: Pole: tuning-fork top with long top bar
text: This tuning fork pole top, with a **long top bar** that sticks out each end and **horizontal bar(s) **below, is found the majority of the time in the Kanto region.

images.caption: Pole beside a house; the red circle zooms in on a tuning-fork top with a long top bar

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A tuning-fork pole top with a long top bar sticking out at each end and bars below it is mostly Kanto.

clues.title: Pole: tuning-fork top with short top bar
text: This tuning fork pole top, with a **short top bar **and **horizontal bar** below, is found the majority of the time in the Chubu region.

images.caption: Pole in the distance; the red circle zooms in on a tuning-fork top with a short top bar

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A tuning-fork pole top with a short top bar and a horizontal bar below is mostly Chubu.

clues.title: Pole: tuning-fork top with thin wire
text: This tuning fork pole top, with a **thin wire** and **horizontal bar **below, is common in the Kansai region.

images.caption: Pole beside a house; the red circle zooms in on a tuning-fork top with a thin wire

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A tuning-fork pole top with a thin wire and a horizontal bar below is common in Kansai.

clues.title: Road: arrow marking the road edge under snow
text: This infrastructural **arrow** informs drivers of where the shoulder line is when under snow, and is located almost exclusively in **Hokkaido**.
NOTE: While much more rare, other variations can be found here:
- This arrow, found in the Aomori prefecture (or more rarely Hokkaido), has distinct [silver bolts](https://goo.gl/maps/Wzi6Ck3BdAB4sY5bA) around the border.
- This variation, found in the Gifu prefecture, is [long and thin](https://goo.gl/maps/fW4rPrBMBpjc1jvw6).
- This alternate [yellow and black](https://goo.gl/maps/JkwqhdWszVzfhDEm6) design can often be found on the northern part of National Highway 275 in Hokkaido.
- This [yellow and green](https://goo.gl/maps/coTFwyXtYaPsfbku6) arrow is found southwest of Sapporo.
- This [yellow and black](https://goo.gl/maps/rsRHBpDVhF9uaHSv9) arrow can be found on Hokkaido.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: An arrow showing drivers where the road edge is under snow, almost only in Hokkaido. Variants: silver bolts around the border in Aomori; long and thin in Gifu; yellow-black on Highway 275; yellow-green southwest of Sapporo.

clues.title: Bollard: flat white with spaced orange reflectors
text: This flat, white bollard, found on the island of Kyushu and in Yamaguchi Prefecture, will have a **series of separated orange reflectors** on one side, and the same white on the opposite.
NOTE: Rarely, you may find similar bollards in Hokkaido. However, both sides will have orange reflectors.

images.caption: White and orange poles; the red circle zooms in on their markings

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A flat white bollard with several separated orange reflectors on one side and plain white on the other, on Kyushu and in Yamaguchi. Rare ones in Hokkaido have orange on both sides.

clues.title: Bollard: black stripe under the reflector
text: Some bollards on the island of Shikoku can have a** black stripe** just under the reflector. They can be found normally, attached to [guardrails](https://goo.gl/maps/dMX9b98ZsCAwWVm27) or [walls](https://goo.gl/maps/ibVKyN6TkXVVCgNm7).

images.caption: Two bollards on a rice field edge: black stripe under the reflector; circle zooms in, arrows point to each

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: On Shikoku some bollards have a black stripe just under the reflector, on their own or attached to guardrails or walls.

clues.title: Bollard: thick, octagon reflector, yellow stripe
text: This **thick**, white bollard, found in the Tohoku region, will have an **octagonal** reflector, and **yellow stripe** just underneath. In addition, you can find the same bollard, but with a [rectangular](https://goo.gl/maps/csG4xahLJ65kQnSf6) top.

Finally, there are two other variations. You can find a black [octagonal](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Sfi2HnuEoh8LvJNW6), and [rectangular](https://goo.gl/maps/DaNEMrzzZ1K42SsW9) version. They are often found on National Highways or Expressways and can have the number printed on them.

images.caption: Pole with an orange ball top and orange stripes; the red circle magnifies the top

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A thick white bollard with an octagonal reflector and a yellow stripe under it, in Tohoku, also with a rectangular top. Black octagonal and rectangular versions exist on national highways and expressways, sometimes with the road number.

clues.title: Bollard: thick, octagon top, two yellow stripes
text: This bollard, much like Tohoku, will be a **thick**, white bollard with an **octagonal** reflector. However, this Akita prefecture variation will have **two yellow stripes **underneath the reflector.

images.caption: Pole with an orange ball top and two orange stripes; the red circle magnifies the top

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Like the Tohoku one: thick, white, octagonal reflector, but with two yellow stripes underneath. This is the Akita version.

clues.title: Bollard: one reflector, extendable, red stripe
text: The Toyama prefecture bollard has **one reflector**, is [**extendable**](https://goo.gl/maps/dYgsuVzTtVHRbVrj7) and has a **red stripe** underneath the reflector.
NOTE: Be careful: if there is either a second reflector, or a yellow stripe instead of a red one, these are different bollards. These are more common variations found across many prefectures.

images.caption: White pole with a red band; the red circle magnifies the top, red-and-white pole beside it

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: One reflector, extendable, with a red stripe under it, in Toyama. A second reflector or a yellow stripe instead is a different, more widespread bollard.

clues.title: Bollard: octagon top, red stripe, sloped base
text: This bollard, with an **octagonal** reflector, and **red stripe** underneath it, is exclusive to the Okayama prefecture. Additionally, there will be a sloped connection where the base meets the reflector.

images.caption: Grey pole with a red stripe under an orange cap; the red circle magnifies the top

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Octagonal reflector with a red stripe under it and a sloped joint between base and reflector, exclusive to Okayama.

clues.title: Bollard: two yellow stripes, one round reflector
text: This bollard, found in the Aomori prefecture, has **two yellow stripes**, a **single circular reflector**, and is **extendable**. Sometimes, only [one thicker stripe](https://goo.gl/maps/FznLNbxyMicDGqgaA) near the top may be present.

images.caption: Pole with orange cap and two yellow stripes; the red circle magnifies the top

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Aomori: two yellow stripes, a single round reflector, and extendable. Sometimes just one thicker stripe near the top.

clues.title: Bollard: striped cover, no reflectors
text: These striped bollards (which cover over the original) have a **thinner** top half, and **no reflectors**, and are common to the Tohoku region. They are especially common in Akita prefecture.

images.caption: Red-and-white striped pole; the red circle magnifies its base

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Striped bollards that cover the original, with a thinner top half and no reflectors, common in Tohoku and especially Akita.

clues.title: Pole: basic thin snow pole
text: In the northern parts of the Chugoku region, you can primarily find these basic snow poles, with either a **thin** **extended**, or **thin contracted** top. They can also sometimes be found in Iwate.

images.caption: A thin snow pole with a round reflector, zoomed in the red circle; a red-and-white pole stands at right

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In northern Chugoku, thin snow poles, extended or contracted, are the usual bollard. Also sometimes in Iwate.

clues.title: Guardrail: green bands
text: Green bands on guardrails are most commonly found in Oita and Miyazaki, but can be found on all of Kyushu.

images.caption: Guardrail post with a green band, centre

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Green bands on guardrails are most common in Oita and Miyazaki, but found across Kyushu.

clues.title: Guardrail: yellow
text: These distinctive **yellow **guardrails can be found in the Yamaguchi Prefecture.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Yellow guardrails are found in Yamaguchi.

clues.title: Guardrail: chevron-like stickers
text: You can find these **chevron-like** stickers, or more rarely orange ones, on guardrails** **in Hokkaido.
- On the [end](https://goo.gl/maps/9JKVotxnj4pqYvLz7) or side of a guardrail.
- Stuck to [metal posts](https://goo.gl/maps/iJBcacVCiaUCobVb8) between wire fences, which are often found in Hokkaido.
- On railings, which are often found on bridges, [underneath](https://goo.gl/maps/S75JPZKg6eYzrfAG6) the inside of the railing.

images.caption: Three roadside markers with chevron-like stickers, each circled in red

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Chevron-like stickers, more rarely orange, on guardrail ends and sides, on metal posts between wire fences, and on bridge railings in Hokkaido.

clues.title: Guardrail: red and yellow striped end stickers
text: Guardrail endings with these **red and yellow** striped stickers can commonly be found across Chugoku, except in Yamaguchi. They can also rarely be found in Niigata.

images.caption: Red and yellow striped sticker on a guardrail end, zoomed in the circle at top left

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Red-and-yellow striped stickers on guardrail ends are common across Chugoku except Yamaguchi, and rarely in Niigata.

clues.title: Traffic light: vertical
text: Vertical traffic lights can be found in Hokkaido, and along the northwestern coast. The usual [horizontal traffic lights](https://goo.gl/maps/wL83475gQqPcevLW9) can be found everywhere else.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Vertical traffic lights are in Hokkaido and along the northwest coast. Horizontal ones are everywhere else.

clues.title: Sign: black with two yellow circles
text: These specific **black **signs with **two yellow circles** are found in Kagawa. Other variations can be seen, including them [stacked](https://goo.gl/maps/vu57GaqMEYEVbA8h6) on top of each other, or with an [arrow attached](https://goo.gl/maps/ijaCjxnsvDk9ohwZ7) above.

images.caption: Black sign with two yellow circles on a roadside post; the red circle zooms in on it

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Black signs with two yellow circles are found in Kagawa, sometimes stacked or with an arrow above.

clues.title: House: kerosene tank, 'Claymore'
text: Kerosine tanks, otherwise known as “Claymores”, can be found more commonly the further **north** you go. They are abundant in Hokkaido, but can be found in prefectures south of it, or in high elevation mountainous areas.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Kerosene tanks (Claymores) get more common going north. They are abundant in Hokkaido and appear in prefectures to the south and in high mountains.

clues.title: House: hot water, gas or propane tanks
text: Hot water, gas and propane tanks can be found more frequently in **northern** prefectures or high elevation mountainous areas. Here are a few common variations you can find:
- The standard [hot water tank](https://goo.gl/maps/WPocxwCcZguGUn9z7).
- [Covered](https://goo.gl/maps/JDeGep9WhjT672Gb6) propane tanks.
- [Exposed](https://goo.gl/maps/ZinuXP8pGdw2bmi89) propane tanks.
- These [cylindrical](https://goo.gl/maps/kGsvLXq7p4ekVuw39) tanks.
- And finally, these [circular](https://goo.gl/maps/8esQoGWDtj3uAwvi8) tripod tanks.
Moreover, these are even more common in rural towns or villages, where major water or gas lines are unavailable.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Hot water, gas and propane tanks are more common in the north and in high mountainous areas, in several shapes.

clues.title: Road: tiny circles that spray warm water
text: Snow prevention roads, known as ‘Shosetsu’, are found mainly in northwest coastal prefectures. They appear as **tiny circles **in the pavement, and spray warm underground water to clear snow.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Snow-prevention roads (Shosetsu) have tiny circles in the pavement that spray warm groundwater to melt snow, mainly on the northwest coast.

clues.title: Road: bike lane, white outside, blue inside
text: Cycling routes in **Ehime** use an outside white, with an inside **blue **line. They are more commonly found along the coast but may be found further inland too.
While exceptions do exist, and can be found in other prefectures, they are the extreme minority.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Cycling routes in Ehime have white on the outside and a blue line inside, more common along the coast. Rare exceptions exist elsewhere.

clues.title: Houses: red-tiled roofs
text: These unique **red-tiled** roofs are most commonly found in **Chugoku**, especially in the prefectures of Hiroshima and Shimane.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: These red-tiled roofs are most common in Chugoku, especially Hiroshima and Shimane.

clues.title: Houses: flat roofs and ladders in the north
text: The further you are **north**, roofs generally transition from tiled to level or flat sloped in order to compensate for heavy snowfall. Northern houses often have **ladders** attached to the side, giving roof access to clear snow.
NOTE: In addition to north to south, high-elevation mountainous regions or high snowfall areas often use such roofs, even in more central or southern prefectures.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Further north, roofs change from tile to flat or low slope for heavy snow, and houses often have a ladder on the side for clearing snow. Snowy mountain areas elsewhere do the same.

clues.title: Houses: white concrete with flat roofs
text: Okinawa can often be recognised by the white concrete buildings with flat roofs.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Okinawa often has white concrete buildings with flat roofs.

clues.title: Plants: giant butterbur leaves by the road
text: [Giant butterbur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petasites_japonicus) (commonly referred to as cabbage) is abundant in **Hokkaido** and some northern prefectures. Plants found south of Hokkaido often have [smaller leaves](https://goo.gl/maps/H79sWvJQ7NUy5EWe9). It is often found growing along the roadside.
NOTE: Cabbage is also found on the island of [Sakhalin](https://goo.gl/maps/cDP6L1rjVAQxszS46), Russia. However, the Google car will not have low-cam there.

images.caption: Red circle marks giant butterbur leaves growing along the roadside

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Giant butterbur (called cabbage) is abundant in Hokkaido and some northern prefectures, with smaller leaves further south. It grows along roadsides. Sakhalin, Russia also has it, but not with a low camera.

differs.how: Russian Sakhalin has no low-cam coverage

clues.title: Plants: tea hedges with frost fans
text: Green tea plants are often grown in hedged rows. You will often see these [fans](https://goo.gl/maps/v7nZn3mNyfSH2Bp19) mounted on poles, which serve the purpose of preventing frost from falling on the plants.
The prefectures of **Shizuoka (36%)** and **Kagoshima (34%)** make up the majority of the production, with Mie (7%), Miyazaki (4%), and other prefectures (17%) making up the minority.

images.caption: Tea hedges with frost fans; circles zoom in on the tea plants and a frost fan blade

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Green tea grows in hedged rows, with fans on poles to keep frost off. Shizuoka (36%) and Kagoshima (34%) grow most of it.

clues.title: Plants: rice paddies, mostly north of Tokyo
text: Rice is mainly produced north of **Tokyo**. During [growth](https://goo.gl/maps/UenU6cmsX3yayDDN7), it resembles straws of grass. And when ready for [harvest](https://goo.gl/maps/xFmiecFYsthvxdeJA), brown husks are visible. They are also commonly planted in [beds of water](https://goo.gl/maps/oroCCdPYkD6zY7CR8).
The regions of Chubu (21%), Kanto (15%), Tohoku (27%), and Hokkaido (7%) make up the majority of production.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Rice is mainly grown north of Tokyo, looks like grass when growing, shows brown husks at harvest, and is often planted in water beds. Tohoku, Chubu, Kanto and Hokkaido grow most of it.

clues.title: Plants: white birch trunks
text: Japanese White Birch grows dominantly in the **Chubu and Hokkaido **regions, and to a lesser extent in Tohoku. Small areas of white birch can be found throughout Japan, so use this information primarily to help assist your region guess.

NOTE: Japanese Beech is another species of tree found in Japan. They, however, have more [grey and spotted bark](https://goo.gl/maps/pA6yUwusCcRfxnSz9), as opposed to the mostly white Japanese White Birch.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Japanese white birch grows mainly in Chubu and Hokkaido, less in Tohoku, with small patches everywhere. Japanese beech has grey, spotted bark instead.

clues.title: Plants: bamboo, more in the south
text: In general, bamboo grows more often in the **south**, and slowly decreases further north. Population size and areas where it grows can vary, so use this information primarily in helping assist your region guess.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bamboo grows more in the south and thins out going north. Use it only to help narrow the region.

clues.title: Plants: Chinese silver grass, abundant on Kyushu
text: Chinese Silver Grass, referred to as Kyushu grass, is indeed very abundant on the island of **Kyushu**. However, use this tip with caution, as they can be seen outside of this area.

NOTE: Another notable region they can be found in is the prefectures of Niigata, Yamagata and Akita. Though, combining the rather large quantity found on Kyushu, its normally distinct vegetation, along with other information, there often will be a clear distinction.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Chinese silver grass is very abundant on Kyushu but also appears elsewhere, notably in Niigata, Yamagata and Akita. Use with care.

clues.title: Plants: sugarcane
text: **Sugarcane** is almost exclusively found on the islands in southern Kyushu and Okinawa.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Sugarcane is almost only on the islands of southern Kyushu and Okinawa.

clues.title: Coverage: little winter coverage in Hokkaido
text: Hokkaido has very **limited** winter and snow coverage. Unless you are certain, it is often better not to guess this prefecture. Though, if you do find yourself in Hokkaido, these regions are most likely. Other low amounts of miscellaneous coverage is primarily in the southern half of the island.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Hokkaido has very little winter and snow coverage, so unless you are sure, don't guess it. Other small amounts of coverage are mainly in the southern half.

clues.title: Landscape: two flat plains
text: Japan is notably a very mountainous country. However, there are some regions that are quite **flat**, being the Nobi and Kanto **plains**. While at times they can look very similar, determining that it is one or the other can be very helpful.
NOTE: While there are, of course, other flat areas in Japan, these two are the most recognizable.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Japan is very mountainous, but the Nobi and Kanto plains are flat. They can look alike, and telling them apart helps.

clues.title: Houses: Shisa guardian lions and house plaques
text: You can find these ‘[Shisa](https://goo.gl/maps/q8uCFQh6YheQ7BdU8)’ guardian lions and house plaques with these [specific characters](https://goo.gl/maps/8sY6Txd3QyUTAKWG8) in Okinawa. The colour and shapes of both can vary.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Shisa guardian lions and house plaques with special characters are found in Okinawa. Colours and shapes vary.

clues.title: Landscape: farm fields with red soil
text: Agricultural fields with red soil are commonly found on several southern islands, most notably on the islands of [Miyakojima ](https://maps.app.goo.gl/p3GiNrHi8rpRptJRA)and [Ishigaki](https://maps.app.goo.gl/DLokgg7yYsaN5yev5) in southern Okinawa.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Red-soil farm fields are common on several southern islands, mostly Miyakojima and Ishigaki in southern Okinawa.

clues.title: Landscape: tall volcano with gentle slope
text: **Mount Fuji** is the tallest mountain in Japan, with a gradual incline and often snowy summit.
Depending on the elevation, it can be seen from far away. This can create some excellent region guesses, especially if you account for direction and distance.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Mount Fuji, the tallest mountain, has a gradual slope and often a snowy top. It can be seen from far away, so direction and distance help.

clues.title: Manhole: five-petal flower with small circles

clues.summary: Tokyo's manhole design has a five-petal flower and many small circles around the edge.
